data:
To eat, like breathing, is a biological instinct of our bodies, necessary for daily functioning. Unlike breathing however, the ways in which we eat, the food items we choose or reject, are linked to societal norms and economic capacities, beyond individual agency. This course will read foodways as systems of communications that encode identities in terms of state and household institutions, geographical markers, religious affiliations, labour and class positions, and caste and gender norms. 
This course will move chronologically through the turn to agriculture, ancient states and empires, religious sacrifices and asceticism, medieval mercantilism, industrialisation and circulation of food and labour, and end in the present day post-globalisation world. We will learn to read primary sources ranging from the pots and pans of the ancient world, medicinal texts, religious canonical literature, oral and written recipe collections, and modern day popular culture. Together, we will use these contexts and sources to understand how food functions as a marker of identity.
